claim: Serious fungal infections result in over 1.5 million deaths annually.
source: Although serious fungal infections are most common in immunocompromised individuals, their impact on global health is still striking, resulting in over 1.5 million deaths annually (Iyer et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Iyer et al., 2022 and Xie et al., 2014

claim: Infectious populations are adapting to available drugs faster than new drugs are developed.
source: How many different molecular mechanisms can a microbe exploit to adapt to a challenging environment? Answering this question is particularly urgent in the field of drug resistance because infectious populations are adapting to available drugs faster than new drugs are developed (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2019, 2019; Ventola, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2019 and Ventola, 2015

claim: Understanding the mechanistic basis of drug resistance can inform strategies for how to combine existing drugs in a way that prevents the evolution of resistance.
source: Understanding the mechanistic basis of drug resistance can inform strategies for how to combine existing drugs in a way that prevents the evolution of resistance (Andersson and Hughes, 2010; Melnikov et al., 2020; Pinheiro et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andersson and Hughes, 2010; Melnikov et al., 2020; Pinheiro et al., 2021

claim: Multi-drug strategies perform best when all mutants that resist Drug A have the same tradeoff in Drug B.
source: Problematically, these multi-drug strategies perform best when all mutants that resist Drug A have the same tradeoff in Drug B (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: If there are multiple different mechanisms to resist Drug A, some of which lack the tradeoff to Drug B, treatment strategies could fail.
source: If there are multiple different mechanisms to resist Drug A, some of which lack this tradeoff, treatment strategies could fail (Figure 1B), and they sometimes do (Abel zur Wiesch et al., 2014; Grier et al., 2003; Scarborough et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in text with supporting citations and illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: Laboratory experiments often find mutants that violate trends or the absence of trends altogether when searching for universal tradeoffs.
source: Laboratory experiments that have power to search for universal tradeoffs – where all the mutants that perform well in one environment perform poorly in another – often find there are mutants that violate trends or the absence of trends altogether (Ardell and Kryazhimskiy, 2021; Gjini and Wood, 2021; Herren and Baym, 2022; Hill et al., 2015; Kinsler et al., 2020; Nichol et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Adaptive mutations often have collateral effects in environments other than the one in which they originally evolved.
source: Another way to phrase this observation is to say that adaptive mutations often have collateral effects in environments other than the one in which they originally evolved (Pál et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pál et al., 2015

claim: Pleiotropic effects of adaptive mutations can be unpredictable and context dependent.
source: But these effects, referred to in some studies as pleiotropic effects, can be unpredictable and context dependent (Bakerlee et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023; Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2020; Hinz et al., 2023; Jerison et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The mutations that provide the strongest fitness advantage often dominate evolution.
source: One reason why is that the mutations that provide the strongest fitness advantage often dominate evolution.
evidence: Based on established evolutionary principles

claim: In the clinic and in laboratory experiments, the same drug-resistant mutations repeatedly emerge.
source: Thus, in the clinic, and in laboratory experiments, the same drug-resistant mutations repeatedly emerge (Berkow and Lockhart, 2017; Ksiezopolska et al., 2021; Lupetti et al., 2002; Melnikov et al., 2020), potentially leading to the false impression that the mechanistic basis of resistance to a particular drug, and the associated tradeoffs, are less varied than may be true.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Bulk DNA sequencing methods often miss mutations that are present in less than 10% of a population's cells.
source: This problem is amplified by the limitations of bulk DNA sequencing methods which often miss mutations that are present in less than 10% of a population's cells (Good et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Good et al., 2017

claim: The lineage-tracing method used has been shown to reveal a fuller spectrum of mutations underlying adaptation to a particular environment.
source: This method has been shown to reveal a fuller spectrum of mutations underlying adaptation to a particular environment (Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Levy et al., 2015

claim: The lineage-tracing method uses DNA barcodes to track all competing adaptive lineages, not just the ones that ultimately rise to appreciable frequency.
source: One key to its success is that it uses DNA barcodes to track all competing adaptive lineages, not just the ones that ultimately rise to appreciable frequency.
evidence: Description of the method's capabilities

claim: The lineage-tracing method captures adaptive lineages before they accumulate multiple mutations such that it is easy to pinpoint which mutation is adaptive.
source: Another key feature is that it captures adaptive lineages before they accumulate multiple mutations such that it is easy to pinpoint which mutation is adaptive.
evidence: Description of the method's capabilities

claim: Previous work has shown that different drug concentrations and combinations select for different azole resistance mechanisms.
source: We did so because previous work has shown that different drug concentrations and combinations select for different azole resistance mechanisms (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005; Hill et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cowen and Lindquist, 2005 and Hill et al., 2015

claim: 774 adaptive yeast strains were obtained in this study.
source: Ultimately, we obtained a large collection of 774 adaptive yeast strains.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental results

claim: Previous work using the same barcoded evolution platform discovered that mutations providing an advantage under glucose-limitation are in genes comprising a canonical glucose-sensing pathway.
source: For example, previous work using the same barcoded evolution platform used here discovered that the mutations that provide an advantage under glucose-limitation are in genes comprising a canonical glucose-sensing pathway (Venkataram et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Venkataram et al., 2016

claim: Despite genetic similarity in glucose-sensing pathway genes, mutants did not experience the same tradeoffs when exposed to new environments.
source: Yet despite this similarity at the genetic level, follow-up work showed that these mutants did not experience the same tradeoffs when exposed to new environments (Kinsler et al., 2020; Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kinsler et al., 2020 and Li et al., 2018b

claim: If two groups of drug resistant mutants have different fitness tradeoffs, it could mean that they provide resistance through different underlying mechanisms.
source: The intuition here is as follows. If two groups of drug resistant mutants have different fitness tradeoffs, it could mean that they provide resistance through different underlying mechanisms.
evidence: Logical reasoning about the relationship between tradeoffs and mechanisms

claim: Previous work is consistent with the idea that mutants with different fitness tradeoffs affect fitness through different underlying mechanisms.
source: Previous work is consistent with the idea that mutants with different fitness tradeoffs affect fitness through different underlying mechanisms (Li et al., 2019; Pinheiro et al., 2021; Rodrigues et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2019; Pinheiro et al., 2021; Rodrigues et al., 2016

claim: Twelve evolution experiments were performed, each starting from the same pool of approximately 300,000 barcoded yeast lineages.
source: We performed a total of 12 barcoded evolution experiments, each of which started from the same pool of approximately 300,000 barcoded yeast lineages (Figure 2A, B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design with supporting figures

claim: The evolutions survey how yeast cells adapt to different concentrations and combinations of fluconazole (FLU) and radicicol (RAD).
source: These evolutions survey how yeast cells adapt to different concentrations and combinations of two drugs: fluconazole (FLU) and radicicol (RAD).
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: Fluconazole is a first line of defense against yeast infections.
source: FLU is a first line of defense against yeast infections, but over the past two decades diverse resistant mutations have been identified (Bongomin et al., 2017; Osset-Trénor et al., 2023; Rybak et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bongomin et al., 2017; Osset-Trénor et al., 2023; Rybak et al., 2022

claim: Over the past two decades diverse resistant mutations to fluconazole have been identified.
source: FLU is a first line of defense against yeast infections, but over the past two decades diverse resistant mutations have been identified (Bongomin et al., 2017; Osset-Trénor et al., 2023; Rybak et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bongomin et al., 2017; Osset-Trénor et al., 2023; Rybak et al., 2022

claim: Some earlier work suggested that FLU-resistant mutants are sensitive to radicicol.
source: Some earlier work suggested that FLU-resistant mutants are sensitive to the second drug we study, radicicol (RAD; Cowen et al., 2009; Cowen and Lindquist, 2005), and more generally that RAD can prevent the emergence of drug resistance in other systems (Whitesell et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cowen et al., 2009; Cowen and Lindquist, 2005; Whitesell et al., 2014

claim: There are some mutants that are cross-resistant to both FLU and RAD.
source: However, there are some mutants that are cross-resistant to both FLU and RAD (Hill et al., 2015), and the prominent mechanism of resistance can differ with the intensity of selection and drug concentration (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005; Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hill et al., 2015; Cowen and Lindquist, 2005; Yang et al., 2023

claim: The prominent mechanism of resistance can differ with the intensity of selection and drug concentration.
source: However, there are some mutants that are cross-resistant to both FLU and RAD (Hill et al., 2015), and the prominent mechanism of resistance can differ with the intensity of selection and drug concentration (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005; Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cowen and Lindquist, 2005; Yang et al., 2023

claim: Approximately 21,000 isolates were sampled from the evolution experiments.
source: We sampled about 2000 cells from each evolution experiment except those three containing high concentrations of FLU from which we sampled only 1000 cells for a total of ~21,000 isolates (2000 cells x 9 conditions +1000 cells x 3 conditions) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure with calculation

claim: Samples were taken from each evolution experiment after 3–6 growth/transfer cycles.
source: With the goal of collecting adaptive lineages from each evolution experiment, we took samples from each one after 3–6 growth/transfer cycles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure

claim: 3–6 growth/transfer cycles represents roughly 24–48 generations of growth assuming 8 generations per growth/transfer cycle.
source: This represents roughly 24–48 generations of growth assuming 8 generations per growth/transfer cycle (Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: Calculation based on cited assumption from Levy et al., 2015

claim: Previous work using this barcoded evolution system demonstrated that the diversity of adaptive lineages peaks after just a few dozen generations.
source: We sampled early because previous work using this barcoded evolution system demonstrated that the diversity of adaptive lineages peaks after just a few dozen generations (Levy et al., 2015; Venkataram et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Levy et al., 2015; Venkataram et al., 2016

claim: The barcoding process is slightly mutagenic.
source: This happens because the barcoding process is slightly mutagenic, thus there is less need to wait for DNA replication errors to introduce mutations (Levy et al., 2015; Venkataram et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Levy et al., 2015; Venkataram et al., 2016

claim: 24 competitive fitness experiments were performed, 2 per each of the original 12 evolution conditions.
source: We performed 24 such competitive fitness experiments, 2 per each of the original 12 evolution conditions (Figure 2E).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design

claim: Fitness was tracked over five growth/transfer cycles (~40 generations) in the competitive fitness experiments.
source: In each experiment, we emulated the growth and transfer conditions of the original evolution experiments as precisely as possible, tracking how barcode frequencies changed over five growth/transfer cycles (~40 generations).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure

claim: 774 lineages with barcodes that were observed >500 times in at least one replicate experiment per each of the 12 conditions were preserved for analysis.
source: We applied a conservative filter, preserving only 774 lineages with barcodes that were observed >500 times in at least one replicate experiment per each of the 12 conditions.
evidence: Direct statement of data filtering procedure

claim: The 774 lineages studied are biased towards those that are reproducibly adaptive in multiple environments.
source: The 774 lineages we focus on are biased towards those that are reproducibly adaptive in multiple environments we study.
evidence: Acknowledgment of experimental bias

claim: By requiring lineages to have high-coverage fitness measurements in all 12 conditions, adaptive mutants that have severe tradeoffs in one or more environments are excluded.
source: By requiring lineages to have high-coverage fitness measurements in all 12 conditions, we exclude adaptive mutants that have severe tradeoffs in one or more environments, consequently blinding ourselves to mutants that act via unique underlying mechanisms.
evidence: Acknowledgment of experimental limitation

claim: Whole genome sequencing was performed on a subset of 53 lineages.
source: To provide additional evidence that these 774 barcoded yeast lineages indeed possess adaptive mutations, we performed whole genome sequencing on a subset of 53 lineages.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure

claim: Each sequenced lineage differs from the ancestor by one or just a few mutations.
source: Because we sampled these lineages after only a few dozen generations of evolution, each lineage differs from the ancestor by one or just a few mutations, making it easy to pinpoint the genetic basis of adaptation.
evidence: Inference based on early sampling timepoint

claim: 35 FLU-resistant yeast lineages were found with unique single nucleotide mutations in either PDR1 or PDR3.
source: For example, we sequenced many FLU-resistant yeast lineages finding 35 with unique single nucleotide mutations in either PDR1 or PDR3, and a few with mutations in SUR1 or UPC2, genes which have all been shown to contribute to FLU resistance in previous work (Flowers et al., 2012; Tanaka and Tani, 2018; Uemura and Moriguchi, 2022; Vasicek et al., 2014; Vu and Moye-Rowley, 2022).
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results with supporting citations

claim: PDR1, PDR3, SUR1, and UPC2 have all been shown to contribute to FLU resistance in previous work.
source: For example, we sequenced many FLU-resistant yeast lineages finding 35 with unique single nucleotide mutations in either PDR1 or PDR3, and a few with mutations in SUR1 or UPC2, genes which have all been shown to contribute to FLU resistance in previous work (Flowers et al., 2012; Tanaka and Tani, 2018; Uemura and Moriguchi, 2022; Vasicek et al., 2014; Vu and Moye-Rowley, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Flowers et al., 2012; Tanaka and Tani, 2018; Uemura and Moriguchi, 2022; Vasicek et al., 2014; Vu and Moye-Rowley, 2022

claim: Lineages with very high fitness in RAD were found to possess single nucleotide mutations in genes associated with RAD resistance, such as HDA1 and HSC82.
source: Similarly, lineages that have very high fitness in RAD were found to possess single nucleotide mutations in genes associated with RAD resistance, such as HDA1 (Robbins et al., 2012) and HSC82, which is the target of RAD (Roe et al., 1999).
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results with supporting citations

claim: HSC82 is the target of RAD.
source: Similarly, lineages that have very high fitness in RAD were found to possess single nucleotide mutations in genes associated with RAD resistance, such as HDA1 (Robbins et al., 2012) and HSC82, which is the target of RAD (Roe et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roe et al., 1999

claim: Several lineages with mutations to IRA1, IRA2, and GPB2 were observed, similar to mutations observed in other studies using this barcoded evolution regime.
source: We also observed several lineages with similar mutations to those observed in other studies using this barcoded evolution regime, including mutations to IRA1, IRA2, and GPB2 (Kinsler et al., 2020; Venkataram et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results with supporting citations

claim: Previous barcoded evolutions observed that increases in ploidy were adaptive, with 43% to 60% of cells becoming diploid during the course of evolution.
source: Previous barcoded evolutions also observed that increases in ploidy were adaptive, with 43% to 60% of cells becoming diploid during the course of evolution (Venkataram et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Venkataram et al., 2016

claim: Ploidy changes contributed less to adaptation in this experiment, with at most 9.4% of cells becoming diploid by the sampling time point.
source: However, ploidy changes contributed less to adaptation in our experiment, with at most 9.4% of cells becoming diploid by the time point when we sampled, but often less than 2% (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental results

claim: The majority of the 774 adaptive lineages have higher fitness than the ancestral strains in several drug conditions.
source: The majority of the 774 adaptive lineages that we study have higher fitness than the ancestral strains in not one, but often in several drug conditions.
evidence: Summary of fitness data

claim: Pleiotropy, and in particular cross-resistance, is prevalent among the lineages studied.
source: This suggests that pleiotropy, and in particular cross-resistance, is prevalent among the lineages we study.
evidence: Inference from fitness data showing advantage in multiple conditions

claim: The 100 most fit lineages in the highest concentration of fluconazole are also beneficial in the highest concentration of radicicol.
source: For example, the 100 most fit lineages in our highest concentration of fluconazole are also beneficial in our highest concentration of radicicol (Figure 3A; leftmost two boxplots).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: The 100 most-fit lineages in high FLU have high fitness in conditions where high concentrations of FLU and RAD are combined.
source: As expected, these 100 lineages also have high fitness in conditions where high concentrations of FLU and RAD are combined (Figure 3A; third boxplot).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: The 100 most-fit lineages in high FLU lose their fitness advantage in conditions where no drug is present.
source: And these 100 most-fit lineages in FLU lose their fitness advantage in conditions where no drug is present (Figure 3A; rightmost boxplot).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: The 100 lineages with highest fitness in high FLU were most often sampled from evolution experiments in which FLU was present.
source: As we expected, these 100 best performing lineages in high FLU largely originate from evolution experiments containing FLU (Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct statement of lineage origin data with supporting figure

claim: The 100 best performing lineages in high FLU are underrepresented in evolution experiments lacking RAD and FLU.
source: Given that these lineages have no fitness advantage in conditions containing no drug, it is also unsurprising that they are underrepresented in evolution experiments lacking RAD and FLU (Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct statement of lineage origin data with supporting figure

claim: Many previous studies find that drug resistant mutants often do not have high fitness in the absence of drug.
source: Further, many previous studies find a similar pattern, whereby drug resistant mutants often do not have high fitness in the absence of drug (Allen et al., 2019; Andersson and Hughes, 2010; Basra et al., 2018; Melnikov et al., 2020), such that treatment strategies have emerged that cycle patients between drug and no drug states, albeit with mixed success (Algazi et al., 2020; Baker et al., 2018; Raymond, 2019; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Drug resistance can sometimes come with an advantage, rather than a cost, in the absence of a drug.
source: However, this type of generalization is not supported by our data. We find that drug resistance can sometimes come with an advantage, rather than a cost, in the absence of a drug (Figure 3C).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: The top 100 most fit mutants in the highest concentration of RAD provide a fitness advantage in high RAD, high FLU, as well as in environments with no drug.
source: The top 100 most fit mutants in our highest concentration of RAD provide a fitness advantage in high RAD, high FLU, as well as in environments with no drug (Figure 3C).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: There are at least two different mechanisms by which to resist FLU that result in different tradeoffs in other environments.
source: These observations suggest that there are at least two different mechanisms by which to resist FLU that result in different tradeoffs in other environments (Figure 3A vs. 3 C).
evidence: Inference from fitness data showing different tradeoff patterns

claim: FLU-resistant lineages that maintain their fitness advantage in the absence of drug mainly originate from evolution experiments performed in conditions lacking FLU.
source: Intriguingly, these FLU-resistant lineages that maintain their fitness advantage in the absence of drug (Figure 3C) mainly originate from evolution experiments performed in conditions lacking FLU (Figure 3D).
evidence: Direct statement of lineage origin data with supporting figures

claim: Typical studies might miss the unique class of FLU-resistant mutants that originate from RAD evolution experiments.
source: This highlights how the potential mechanisms by which a microbe can resist a drug may be more varied than is often believed. Typically, one does not search for FLU-resistant mutants by evolving yeast to resist RAD. Thus typical studies might miss this unique class of FLU-resistant mutants.
evidence: Inference about limitations of typical experimental approaches

claim: One group of mutants has almost equally high fitness in RAD and FLU but has no fitness advantage over the ancestral strain in conditions without either drug.
source: One group has almost equally high fitness in RAD and FLU but has no fitness advantage over the ancestral strain in conditions without either drug (Figure 3A).
evidence: Summary of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: Another group of mutants is defined by very high fitness in RAD, moderately high fitness in FLU and moderately high fitness in conditions without either drug.
source: Another group is defined by very high fitness in RAD, moderately high fitness in FLU and moderately high fitness in conditions without either drug (Figure 3C).
evidence: Summary of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: When comparing fitness in RAD vs. FLU across all 774 lineages, they largely fall into two main categories.
source: When comparing fitness in RAD vs. FLU across all 774 lineages, not only the top 100 best performing in each drug, we see some evidence that they largely fall into the two main categories highlighted in Figure 3A and C (Figure 3E).
evidence: Direct statement of data analysis with supporting figure

claim: Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) was applied to fitness measurements for 774 yeast strains across all 12 environments.
source: To see whether there are distinct fitness profiles present among our drug-resistant yeast lineages, we applied uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP)to fitness measurements for 774 yeast strains across all 12 environments.
evidence: Direct statement of analysis method

claim: UMAP places mutants with similar fitness profiles near each other in two-dimensional space.
source: This method places mutants with similar fitness profiles near each other in two-dimensional space.
evidence: Description of UMAP method

claim: A gaussian mixture model (GMM) was used to identify clusters on the UMAP.
source: Beyond the obvious divide between the top and bottom clusters of mutants on the UMAP, we used a gaussian mixture model (GMM; Fraley and Raftery, 2003) to identify clusters.
evidence: Direct statement of analysis method with citation

claim: Seven clusters of distinct mutants were identified, including one pertaining to the control strains, and six others pertaining to presumed different classes of adaptive mutant.
source: Using this information, we identified seven clusters of distinct mutants, including one pertaining to the control strains, and six others pertaining to presumed different classes of adaptive mutant (Figure 4D).
evidence: Direct statement of clustering results with supporting figure

claim: Fitness was calculated as the slope of the log-linear change in barcode frequency relative to the average slope of the control strains.
source: Therefore, we calculated fitness via the traditional method, as the slope of the log-linear change in barcode frequency relative to the average slope of the control strains.
evidence: Direct statement of fitness calculation method

claim: Fitness inferences were reproducible between replicates.
source: Using this method, we found that our fitness inferences were reproducible between replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), and between experiments performed in similar conditions (e.g. medium vs. high concentrations of the same drug; Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Direct statement of reproducibility with supporting figures

claim: When the coverage threshold was increased from 500 to 5000 reads per lineage, 157 lineages were lost (from 774 to 617).
source: When we increased our coverage threshold to require an order of magnitude more reads per lineage per measurement (from 500 to 5000), we lost 157 lineages (from 774 to 617), saw reproducibility increase across replicates (from an average Pearson correlation of 0.756–0.813) and the main conclusions of our study were unchanged in that the same 6 clusters were present on a UMAP (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement of data filtering results with supporting figure

claim: Reproducibility increased across replicates when coverage threshold was increased (from an average Pearson correlation of 0.756 to 0.813).
source: When we increased our coverage threshold to require an order of magnitude more reads per lineage per measurement (from 500 to 5000), we lost 157 lineages (from 774 to 617), saw reproducibility increase across replicates (from an average Pearson correlation of 0.756–0.813) and the main conclusions of our study were unchanged in that the same 6 clusters were present on a UMAP (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement of reproducibility analysis with supporting figure

claim: 122 colonies were randomly picked and sequenced.
source: In total 122 colonies were randomly picked and sequenced.
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing procedure

claim: Of the 122 genomes sequenced, only 53 had unique barcodes that pertained to the 774 lineages for which high enough barcode coverage was obtained to infer fitness.
source: Of the 122 genomes we sequenced, only 53 had unique barcodes that pertained to the 774 lineages for which we obtained high enough barcode coverage to infer fitness.
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results

claim: Only two of the 53 sequenced lineages had no sequenced mutations suggesting their fitness increase over ancestor is due to a mutation unable to be identified by sequencing.
source: Only two of these 53 had no sequenced mutations suggesting their fitness increase over ancestor is due to a mutation we are unable to identify by sequencing, perhaps a change in ploidy.
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results with speculation about cause

claim: The other 51 sequenced lineages all had at least one single nucleotide mutation in a gene reported in Supplementary file 1.
source: The other 51 all had at least one single nucleotide mutation in a gene reported in Supplementary file 1.
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results

claim: Cluster 1 is unique in that it does not contain mutations to PDR1 or PDR3.
source: For example, in cluster 1 (depicted in purple in Figures 4 and 5), the three sequenced lineages have single nucleotide mutations to either SUR1 or UPC2 (Figure 5A). But in clusters 2 and 3 (depicted in blue and orange in Figures 4 and 5), 35/36 sequenced lineages have unique single nucleotide mutations to one of two genes associated with 'Pleiotropic Drug Resistance' (PDR1 or PDR3).
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results with supporting figures

claim: In clusters 2 and 3, 35/36 sequenced lineages have unique single nucleotide mutations to PDR1 or PDR3.
source: But in clusters 2 and 3 (depicted in blue and orange in Figures 4 and 5), 35/36 sequenced lineages have unique single nucleotide mutations to one of two genes associated with 'Pleiotropic Drug Resistance' (PDR1 or PDR3).
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results with supporting figures

claim: PDR1 and PDR3 are transcription factors that contribute to fluconazole resistance through increased transcription of a drug pump (PDR5) that removes FLU from cells.
source: PDR1 and PDR3 are transcription factors that are well known to contribute to fluconazole resistance through increased transcription of a drug pump (PDR5) that removes FLU from cells (Fardeau et al., 2007; Osset-Trénor et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fardeau et al., 2007; Osset-Trénor et al., 2023

claim: SUR1 converts inositol phosphorylceramide to mannosylinositol phosphorylceramide, which is a component of the plasma membrane.
source: SUR1 converts inositol phosphorylceramide to mannosylinositol phosphorylceramide, which is a component of the plasma membrane (Uemura and Moriguchi, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uemura and Moriguchi, 2022

claim: UPC2 is a transcription factor with a key role in activating the ergosterol biosynthesis genes, which contribute to membrane formation.
source: Similarly, UPC2 is a transcription factor with a key role in activating the ergosterol biosynthesis genes, which contribute to membrane formation (Tan et al., 2022; Rine, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tan et al., 2022; Rine, 2001

claim: The presence of adaptive mutations in genes involved in membrane synthesis is consistent with fluconazole's disruptive effect on membranes.
source: The presence of adaptive mutations in genes involved in membrane synthesis is consistent with fluconazole's disruptive effect on membranes (Sorgo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sorgo et al., 2011

claim: Lineages with mutations to UPC2 and SUR1 do not consistently have cross-resistance in RAD.
source: Interestingly, the lineages with mutations to UPC2 and SUR1, and the unsequenced lineages in the same cluster, do not consistently have cross-resistance in RAD (Figure 5B; cluster 1).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: Lineages with mutations to PDR1 or PDR3 are uniformly cross-resistant to RAD.
source: Oppositely, lineages with mutations to PDR1 or PDR3, and the unsequenced lineages in the same clusters, are uniformly cross-resistant to RAD (Figure 5B; clusters 2 and 3).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: The drug efflux pump that PDR1/3 regulates (PDR5) can transport a wide range of drugs and molecules out of yeast cells.
source: Perhaps, this cross-resistance is reflective of the fact that the drug efflux pump that PDR1/3 regulates (PDR5) can transport a wide range of drugs and molecules out of yeast cells (Harris et al., 2021; Kolaczkowski et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris et al., 2021; Kolaczkowski et al., 1996

claim: The lineages in cluster 1 perform best in the lowest concentration of FLU and have decreasing fitness as the concentration of FLU rises.
source: The lineages in cluster 1 perform best in the lowest concentration of FLU and have decreasing fitness as the concentration of FLU rises (Figure 5C).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: About 15% of cluster 1 mutant lineages perform worse than their ancestor in the highest concentration of FLU.
source: In fact, about 15% of these mutant lineages perform worse than their ancestor in the highest concentration of FLU, suggesting the very mutations that provide resistance to low FLU are costly in higher concentrations of the same drug.
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data

claim: The mutants in clusters 2 and 3 perform best in the highest concentration of FLU and have reduced fitness in lower concentrations.
source: The mutants in clusters 2 and 3 show the opposite trend from those in cluster 1. They perform best in the highest concentration of FLU and have reduced fitness in lower concentrations (Figure 5C).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: Mutants in cluster 1 predominantly originated in evolutions containing the lowest concentration of FLU.
source: Mutants in cluster 1 predominantly originated in evolutions containing the lowest concentration of FLU (Figure 5A; pie charts), while mutants in clusters 2 and 3 more often originated from evolution experiments containing higher FLU concentrations (see Figure 6).
evidence: Direct statement of lineage origin data with supporting figures

claim: Lineages from cluster 1 (SUR1, UPC2) grow faster and reach higher density in low FLU than those from cluster 3 (PDR).
source: Lineages from cluster 1 (SUR1, UPC2) indeed grow faster and reach higher density in low FLU than those from cluster 3 (PDR; Figure 5D).
evidence: Direct statement of growth curve data with supporting figure

claim: Lineages from cluster 1 (SUR1, UPC2) grow poorly in higher FLU concentrations, while lineages from cluster 3 (PDR) do not suffer this tradeoff.
source: But lineages from cluster 1 (SUR1, UPC2) grow poorly in higher FLU concentrations, while lineages from cluster 3 (PDR) do not suffer this tradeoff (Figure 5E).
evidence: Direct statement of growth curve data with supporting figure

claim: The mutants in clusters 2 and 3 have fitness profiles with a very similar shape.
source: For one, the mutants in clusters 2 and 3 have fitness profiles with a very similar shape (Figures 4E and 6A).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness profile analysis with supporting figures

claim: The sequenced lineages in clusters 2 and 3 possess mutations to the same genes: PDR1 and PDR3.
source: The sequenced lineages in each of these clusters also possess mutations to the same genes: PDR1 and PDR3 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results with supporting figure

claim: The lineages in clusters 2 and 3 originate from similar evolution experiments, largely those containing FLU.
source: And finally, the lineages in each cluster originate from similar evolution experiments, largely those containing FLU (Figure 6A; pie charts).
evidence: Direct statement of lineage origin data with supporting figure

claim: After normalizing fitness profiles to have the same height, clusters 2 and 3 were not merged into a single cluster.
source: To investigate this idea, we normalized all fitness profiles to have the same height on the vertical axis; this does not affect their shape (Figure 6A; dotted lines). Then we re-clustered and asked whether mutants pertaining to the original clusters 2 and 3 were now merged into a single cluster. They were not (Figure 6B).
evidence: Direct statement of clustering analysis results with supporting figures

claim: 37% of mutants in the original clusters 2 and 3 switched from one of these two groups to the other after normalization.
source: Clusters 2 and 3, containing lineages with mutations to PDR1 or PDR 3, experienced the largest changes with 37% of mutants switching from one of these two groups to the other.
evidence: Direct statement of clustering analysis results

claim: Mutants in cluster 3 perform better in high and medium concentrations of RAD compared to cluster 2.
source: For example, mutants in cluster 3 perform better in high and medium concentrations of RAD (Figure 6B; line plot).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: More mutant lineages in cluster 3 originated from the evolutions performed in RAD compared to cluster 2.
source: This difference in fitness is reflected in the evolution experiments, with more mutant lineages in cluster 3 originating from the evolutions performed in RAD (Figure 6B; pie charts).
evidence: Direct statement of lineage origin data with supporting figure

claim: Cluster 3 mutants tend to have reduced fitness in conditions containing neither FLU nor RAD as compared to cluster 2 lineages.
source: Though cluster 3 mutants tend to have stronger RAD resistance, they tend to have reduced fitness in conditions containing neither FLU nor RAD as compared to cluster 2 lineages (Figure 6B; line plot).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: Others have recently observed that mutants to PDR1 do not all behave the same way when exposed to novel drugs or changes in pH.
source: Others have also recently observed that mutants to PDR1 do not all behave the same way when exposed to novel drugs or changes in pH (Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2023

claim: Adaptive missense mutations to IRA1 do not share similarly shaped fitness profiles.
source: This phenomenon is not reserved to PDR mutants, as adaptive missense mutations to another gene, IRA1, also do not share similarly shaped fitness profiles either (Kinsler et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kinsler et al., 2020

claim: Previous work demonstrating that mutations commonly affect multiple traits supports a broader view of the mechanistic differences between clusters.
source: Previous work demonstrating that mutations commonly affect multiple traits supports this broader view of the mechanistic differences between clusters (Boyle et al., 2017; Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2020; Kinsler et al., 2020; Paaby and Rockman, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boyle et al., 2017; Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2020; Kinsler et al., 2020; Paaby and Rockman, 2013

claim: PDR1 and PDR3 regulate transcription of YOR1 and SNQ2 as well as PDR5.
source: PDR1 and PDR3 regulate transcription of YOR1 and SNQ2 as well as PDR5, and maybe the different clusters we observe represent mutants that upregulate one of these downstream targets more than the other (Osset-Trénor et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Osset-Trénor et al., 2023

claim: The three clusters of mutants on the bottom half of the UMAP are all advantageous in RAD and in conditions without any drug.
source: Although the three clusters of mutants on the bottom half of the UMAP are all advantageous in RAD and in conditions without any drug (Figure 4E; lower three plots), they differ in their fitness in conditions containing FLU.
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: The cluster of yeast lineages in cluster 4 is unique in that it has a slight advantage in the HRLF environment.
source: For example, the cluster of yeast lineages highlighted in green (cluster 4 in Figures 4 and 7A) is unique in that it has a slight advantage in the HRLF environment (Figure 7B).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figures

claim: Mutants in cluster 5 do not have a fitness advantage in the HRLF condition despite having advantages in the LF and HR single drug conditions.
source: We found it especially strange that the neighboring cluster 5 does not also have a fitness advantage in this condition. Mutants in cluster 5 have a slight advantage in the LF condition, and a big advantage in the HR condition, thus we expect them to have at least some fitness advantage in the condition where these two drugs are combined (HRLF), but they do not (Figure 7B).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: Cluster 5 mutants have an advantage in both LRLF single drug conditions which is lost when the drugs are combined.
source: The same is true for the combination of LRLF: cluster 5 mutants have an advantage in both single drug conditions which is lost when the drugs are combined (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: The mutants in cluster 4 exhibit no sensitivity to combined treatment, preserving their advantage in multidrug conditions.
source: However, the mutants in cluster 4 (green) exhibit no such sensitivity to combined treatment. They have a slight advantage in all of the aforementioned single drug conditions, which is preserved in the relevant multidrug conditions (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figures

claim: About 10% of cluster 4 lineages originated from the HRLF evolution, while almost none of the lineages in cluster 5 came from this experiment.
source: About 10% of cluster 4 lineages originated from the HRLF evolution, while almost none of the lineages in cluster 5 came from this experiment, confirming that cluster 5 lineages are uniquely sensitive to this multidrug environment (Figure 7C).
evidence: Direct statement of lineage origin data with supporting figure

claim: The selected mutants in cluster 4 and 5 appear to have markedly different growth curves in some conditions.
source: Indeed, the selected mutants in cluster 4 and 5 appear to have markedly different growth curves in some conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement of growth curve data with supporting figure

claim: The cluster 5 mutant has a lower maximum growth rate in the HRLF multidrug condition, corresponding with their lower fitness in this condition.
source: For example, the cluster 5 mutant has a lower maximum growth rate in the HRLF multidrug condition, corresponding with their lower fitness in this condition (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: Direct statement of growth curve and fitness data with supporting figures

claim: The cluster 5 mutant reaches a lower maximum cell density in the LRLF multidrug condition and also has lower fitness in this condition.
source: The cluster 5 mutant also reaches a lower maximum cell density in the LRLF multidrug condition and also has lower fitness in this condition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement of growth curve and fitness data with supporting figure

claim: Cluster 6 has the largest fitness advantage in conditions lacking any drug compared to the other two clusters in the lower half of the UMAP.
source: One group of mutants in the lower half of the UMAP (cluster 6 in Figure 8A) appears distinct from the other two in that it has the largest fitness advantage in conditions lacking any drug (Figure 8B).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figures

claim: Over 50% of the lineages in cluster 6 were sampled from the 'no drug' and 'DMSO' control evolution experiments.
source: Indeed, this is what we observe: over 50% of the lineages in cluster 6 were sampled from one of these two evolution experiments (Figure 8A).
evidence: Direct statement of lineage origin data with supporting figure

claim: The other clusters in the lower half of the UMAP consist mainly of lineages sampled from one of the RAD evolutions.
source: On the contrary, the other clusters in the lower half of the UMAP consist mainly of lineages sampled from one of the RAD evolutions (Figure 7C).
evidence: Direct statement of lineage origin data with supporting figure

claim: The five sequenced mutants in cluster 6 include three that have mutations to IRA1.
source: In line with the success of cluster 6 mutants in no drug conditions, the five sequenced mutants in this cluster include three that have mutations to IRA1, which was the most common target of adaptation in another evolution experiment in the condition we call 'no drug' (Figure 8A; Venkataram et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results with supporting figure and citation

claim: IRA1 was the most common target of adaptation in another evolution experiment in the 'no drug' condition.
source: In line with the success of cluster 6 mutants in no drug conditions, the five sequenced mutants in this cluster include three that have mutations to IRA1, which was the most common target of adaptation in another evolution experiment in the condition we call 'no drug' (Figure 8A; Venkataram et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Venkataram et al., 2016

claim: In the no drug experiment, mutations to IRA1 result in a greater fitness advantage than mutations to its paralog, IRA2, or mutations to other negative regulators of the RAS/PKA pathway such as GPB2.
source: In that experiment, and in our no drug experiment, mutations to IRA1 result in a greater fitness advantage than mutations to its paralog, IRA2, or mutations to other negative regulators of the RAS/PKA pathway such as GPB2 (Figure 8).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: Previous work showed that sometimes IRA1 mutants have very strong tradeoffs, becoming extremely maladaptive in environments containing salt or benomyl.
source: Previous work showed that sometimes IRA1 mutants have very strong tradeoffs, for example, they become extremely maladaptive in environments containing salt or benomyl (Kinsler et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kinsler et al., 2020

claim: IRA1 mutants do not have extreme tradeoffs in FLU or RAD, maintaining a fitness advantage in the highest concentration of both drugs.
source: We do not observe this to be the case for either FLU or RAD. In fact, we observe that cluster 6 mutants, including those in IRA1, maintain a fitness advantage in our highest concentration of both drugs (Figure 4), being more fit in high FLU than mutants in either of the other clusters in the lower half of the UMAP (Figure 8B).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figures

claim: Cluster 6 mutants are unique in that they lose their fitness advantage in the lowest concentration of FLU.
source: However, cluster 6 mutants are unique in that they lose their fitness advantage in the lowest concentration of FLU (Figure 8B).
evidence: Direct statement of fitness data with supporting figure

claim: The 774 FLU-resistant mutants studied clustered into 6 groups with characteristic tradeoffs.
source: The 774 FLU-resistant mutants studied here clustered into a handful of groups (6) with characteristic tradeoffs.
evidence: Summary of clustering analysis results

claim: Some groupings segregate mutations within the same gene.
source: Some groupings are unintuitive in that they segregate mutations within the same gene (Figure 6) or are distinguished by unexpectedly low fitness in multidrug conditions (Figure 7).
evidence: Summary of clustering results with supporting figures

claim: Some groupings are distinguished by unexpectedly low fitness in multidrug conditions.
source: Some groupings are unintuitive in that they segregate mutations within the same gene (Figure 6) or are distinguished by unexpectedly low fitness in multidrug conditions (Figure 7).
evidence: Summary of clustering results with supporting figures

claim: These findings challenge strategies in evolutionary medicine that rely on consistent tradeoffs or intuitive trends when designing sequential drug treatments.
source: These findings are important because they challenge strategies in evolutionary medicine that rely on consistent tradeoffs or intuitive trends when designing sequential drug treatments.
evidence: Inference about implications of findings

claim: The observation that some mutants have very similar tradeoffs such that they cluster together suggests predicting the impact of some mutations by understanding the impacts of others is somewhat feasible.
source: On the other hand, the observation that some mutants have very similar tradeoffs such that they cluster together is promising in that it suggests predicting the impact of some mutations by understanding the impacts of others is somewhat feasible.
evidence: Inference about implications of findings

claim: Additional FLU-resistant mutants emerge from evolution experiments in conditions lacking FLU.
source: Problematically, the clusters we present are incomplete and bound to change as additional data presents itself. For one, we have shown that additional FLU-resistant mutants emerge from evolution experiments in conditions lacking FLU (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Direct statement of findings with supporting figures

claim: Previous work has shown that some mutants that group together in this study (e.g. GPB2 and IRA2) have different fitness profiles in conditions not included here.
source: Additionally, previous work has shown that some mutants that group together in our study (e.g. GPB2 and IRA2) have different fitness profiles in conditions that we did not include here (Kinsler et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kinsler et al., 2020

claim: The evolution experiments were conducted for only a few generations and all started from the same genetic background.
source: Also of note is that our evolution experiments were conducted for only a few generations and all started from the same genetic background.
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: Additional types of FLU-resistant mutants with unique fitness profiles may emerge from other genetic backgrounds or arise after more mutations are allowed to accumulate.
source: Additional types of FLU-resistant mutants with unique fitness profiles may emerge from other genetic backgrounds or arise after more mutations are allowed to accumulate (Allen et al., 2021; Bosch et al., 2021; Brandis et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to Allen et al., 2021; Bosch et al., 2021; Brandis et al., 2012

claim: The study is underpowered to detect adaptive lineages that have low fitness in any of the 12 environments.
source: Finally, by requiring that all included mutants have sufficient sequencing coverage in all 12 environments, our study is underpowered to detect adaptive lineages that have low fitness in any of the 12 environments.
evidence: Acknowledgment of experimental limitation

claim: Previous work has shown some FLU resistant mutants have strong tradeoffs in RAD.
source: For example, previous work has shown some FLU resistant mutants have strong tradeoffs in RAD (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cowen and Lindquist, 2005

claim: There are more unique types of FLU-resistant mutations than those represented by the 6 clusters identified.
source: All of the aforementioned observations combined suggest that there are more unique types of FLU-resistant mutations than those represented by these 6 clusters, and that the molecular mechanisms that can contribute to fitness in FLU are more diverse than we know.
evidence: Inference from limitations and observations

claim: Not every infection harbors all possible types of mutants.
source: On the up side for evolutionary medicine, not every infection harbors all possible types of mutants.
evidence: General statement about infection biology

claim: Strategies that exploit one or two common tradeoffs have some, albeit mixed, success in delaying or preventing the emergence of resistance.
source: This might explain why strategies that exploit one or two common tradeoffs have some, albeit mixed, success in delaying or preventing the emergence of resistance (Amin et al., 2015; Imamovic et al., 2018; Kaiser, 2017; Krishna et al., 2022; Nyhoegen and Uecker, 2023; Waller et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Amin et al., 2015; Imamovic et al., 2018; Kaiser, 2017; Krishna et al., 2022; Nyhoegen and Uecker, 2023; Waller et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019

claim: The findings support that nuanced strategies to forestall resistance that allow for multiple mutant types may be feasible.
source: Our findings support that such ideas may be feasible by demonstrating that there are not as many unique fitness tradeoffs as there are mutations.
evidence: Inference from findings about number of clusters vs. number of mutations

claim: The work contributes to growing literature suggesting that the phenotypic basis of adaptation is not as diverse as the genetic basis.
source: More generally, our work – showing that 774 mutants fall into a much smaller number of groups – contributes to growing literature suggesting that the phenotypic basis of adaptation is not as diverse as the genetic basis (Iwasawa et al., 2022; Kinsler et al., 2020; Petti et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Iwasawa et al., 2022; Kinsler et al., 2020; Petti et al., 2023

claim: The winnowing of diversity from 774 mutants to 6 groups may mean that evolutionary processes are sometimes predictable.
source: This winnowing of diversity is important: it may mean that evolutionary processes, for example, whether an infectious population will adapt to resist a drug, are sometimes predictable (King et al., 2022; Kinsler et al., 2020; Lässig et al., 2017; Rodrigues et al., 2016; Wortel et al., 2023; Yoon et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to King et al., 2022; Kinsler et al., 2020; Lässig et al., 2017; Rodrigues et al., 2016; Wortel et al., 2023; Yoon et al., 2021

claim: All budding yeast lineages studied originated from the same starting strain referred to as the 'landing pad strain' (SHA185).
source: All of the budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) lineages studied here originated from the same starting strain referred to as the 'landing pad strain' (SHA185) in previous work (Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental materials with citation

claim: All experiments were conducted in 'M3' media, which is a glucose-limited media lacking uracil.
source: All experiments were conducted in 'M3' media defined in the same study as the landing pad strain (Levy et al., 2015), which is a glucose-limited media lacking uracil.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental conditions with citation

claim: A 'low' concentration of each drug was chosen that appeared to have no effect on growth rate.
source: Ultimately, we chose a 'low' concentration of each drug that appeared to have no effect on growth rate, and a 'high' concentration that appeared to reduce growth rate by about 15% (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design with supporting figure

claim: A 'high' concentration of each drug was chosen that appeared to reduce growth rate by about 15%.
source: Ultimately, we chose a 'low' concentration of each drug that appeared to have no effect on growth rate, and a 'high' concentration that appeared to reduce growth rate by about 15% (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design with supporting figure

claim: 5 μM was chosen as the low RAD concentration because previous work suggested this concentration had widespread effects on yeast physiology without affecting growth.
source: Although the lowest concentration of radicicol that we tested on a plate reader was 10 μM, we chose 5 μM as our low RAD concentration because previous work suggested this concentration had widespread effects on yeast physiology without affecting growth (Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2016; Jarosz and Lindquist, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2016; Jarosz and Lindquist, 2010

claim: The barcodes are 25 base pairs in length.
source: These barcodes are 25 base pairs in length.
evidence: Direct statement of barcode characteristics

claim: The barcodes are targeted to an artificial intron within the Ura3 gene.
source: They are targeted to an artificial intron within the Ura3 gene, such that they must be retained in media lacking uracil but are not expressed and thus do not themselves affect fitness (Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement of barcode design with citation

claim: The barcodes must be retained in media lacking uracil but are not expressed and thus do not themselves affect fitness.
source: They are targeted to an artificial intron within the Ura3 gene, such that they must be retained in media lacking uracil but are not expressed and thus do not themselves affect fitness (Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Levy et al., 2015

claim: 24 separate transformations were performed and pooled to obtain a large pool of barcoded yeast.
source: Ultimately we performed 24 separate transformations and pooled many of these to obtain a large pool of barcoded yeast where every yeast cell was genetically identical except for its DNA barcode.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure

claim: Monster lineages were defined as lineages representing greater than 1% of all transformants.
source: Therefore, our final library of barcoded lineages was created by pooling 14 individual transformations together, choosing those 14 that lacked monster lineages, which we defined as lineages representing greater than 1% of all transformants.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental criteria

claim: The final barcode library contains about 300,000 unique barcodes.
source: Our sequencing results suggest that this library contains about 300,000 unique barcodes.
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results

claim: The evolution experiments were completed for a total of 24 growth/transfer cycles, corresponding to 192 generations of growth.
source: We completed a total of 24 growth/transfer cycles, corresponding to 192 generations of growth assuming 8 generations per 48 hr cycle (Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure with calculation

claim: The barcodeless ancestor strain was created by transforming SHA185 with a linear piece of DNA such that the genetic background was identical to the strains of the barcoded library, but the homology to the primers used to amplify the barcode was missing.
source: This strain was created by transforming SHA185 with a linear piece of DNA such that the genetic background was identical to the strains of the barcoded library, but the homology to the primers used to amplify the barcode was missing.
evidence: Direct statement of strain construction procedure

claim: In this barcoded evolution platform, most mutations occur during the transformation that introduces the DNA barcodes.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that in this evolution platform, most mutations occur during the transformation that introduces the DNA barcodes (Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Levy et al., 2015

claim: Secondary mutations have a minimal influence on fitness in this experimental system.
source: For a detailed treatment of how secondary mutations have a minimal influence on fitness, see Venkataram et al., 2016.
evidence: Supported by citation to Venkataram et al., 2016

claim: Whole genome sequences were deposited in GenBank under SRA reference PRJNA1023288.
source: Whole genome sequences were deposited in GenBank under SRA reference PRJNA1023288.
evidence: Direct statement of data deposition

claim: Fitness measurements from each of the 12 environments were normalized to have the same overall mean and variance before performing dimensional reduction.
source: In order to prevent conditions with the most variation in fitness (e.g. high FLU) from dominating, we normalized fitness measurements from each of the 12 environments to have the same overall mean and variance (we transformed the data from every environment to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1) before performing dimensional reduction.
evidence: Direct statement of data normalization procedure

claim: The clustering of mutants was robust to different decisions made when choosing how to analyze the data.
source: In short, the clustering of mutants was robust to the different decisions we made when choosing how to analyze these data.
evidence: Summary statement about robustness of clustering

claim: For most clusters, over 80% of lineages from the UMAP cluster corresponded with a unique hierarchical cluster.
source: We found that, for most clusters, over 80% of lineages from the UMAP cluster corresponded with a unique hierarchical cluster and labeled these hierarchical clusters according to this correspondence (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Direct statement of clustering comparison results with supporting figure

claim: 85% of lineages from each UMAP cluster are clustered together in the corresponding hierarchical cluster when considering cluster 1 mutants in cluster 3/7 as 'mis-clustered'.
source: If we consider these cluster 1 mutants that end up in cluster 3/7 as 'mis-clustered', we find that 85% of lineages from each UMAP cluster are clustered together in the corresponding hierarchical cluster.
evidence: Direct statement of clustering comparison results

claim: 90% of lineages are correctly clustered when considering cluster 1 mutants in cluster 3/7 as 'consistently clustered'.
source: If we consider these as 'consistently clustered', this metric increases to 90% of lineages correctly clustered.
evidence: Direct statement of clustering comparison results
